title: The Crowd
author: Gustave Le Bon
public_title: Why we believe what impressive people say | Gustave Le Bon
hook: Why do we so often believe something because an impressive person said it?
source_kind: Original MindLore commentary on retained passages of the original; limitations and later criticism discussed; owner review required

source_passages.excerpt: Prestige in reality is a sort of domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea.
The various kinds of prestige may be grouped under two principal heads: acquired prestige and personal prestige.

Personal prestige, on the contrary, is something essentially peculiar to the individual; it may coexist with reputation, glory, and fortune, or be strengthened by them, but it is perfectly capable of existing in their absence.

Crowds are only cognisant of simple and extreme sentiments; the opinions, ideas, and beliefs suggested to them are accepted or rejected as a whole, and considered as absolute truths or as not less absolute errors.

Being in doubt as to what constitutes truth or error, and having, on the other hand, a clear notion of its strength, a crowd is as disposed to give authoritative effect to its inspirations as it is intolerant.
To belong to a school is necessarily to espouse its prejudices and preconceived opinions.
Great power is given to ideas propagated by affirmation, repetition, and contagion by the circumstance that they acquire in time that mysterious force known as prestige.

sections.title: Why impressive people persuade us
sections.narration: Why do we so often believe something because an impressive person said it? Gustave Le Bon gives the effect a name in The Crowd, published in 1895. He calls it prestige. He says prestige in reality is a sort of domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea. Think of a famous expert whose opinion you accept before you check it, or a classic book you praise without having read it. That quiet pull is what Le Bon is describing. He did not mean admiration for good reasons. He meant a kind of respect that works before evaluation begins. This is our second video on The Crowd, and it follows a different thread from the first, which was about group feeling. Here we ask how authority and reputation shape belief. As always, we should read him critically. He wrote in the 1890s, with strong opinions about politics, and modern researchers have tested the effects of authority more carefully. The question is still a good one for everyday judgment.

sections.title: Two kinds of prestige
sections.narration: Le Bon sorts prestige into two kinds. He says the various kinds of prestige may be grouped under two principal heads, acquired prestige and personal prestige. Acquired prestige comes from a name, a title, or a position. A person in a white coat or behind a podium receives it before saying a word. Personal prestige is different, and belongs to the individual. This distinction is practical. When you meet a claim, you can ask which kind of prestige is carrying it. Is the speaker persuasive because of a title they hold, or because their reasoning holds up? Both kinds can mislead, and both can also be earned. A real expert deserves some trust, since checking everything yourself is impossible. The skill is to match trust to evidence. Ask whether the person has a track record in this exact subject, and whether others who know the field agree. A title is a reason to listen carefully. It is not, by itself, a reason to believe.

sections.title: Prestige that needs no fortune
sections.narration: Le Bon makes a careful point about personal prestige. He writes that it is something essentially peculiar to the individual, that it may coexist with reputation, glory, and fortune, or be strengthened by them, but that it is perfectly capable of existing in their absence. In other words, a person can command respect without wealth or fame. Think of a teacher whom students trust, or a neighbor everyone consults. Their influence rests on something other than status. Le Bon thinks this quality is rare and hard to explain, and here his account is vague. He does not say clearly what makes it up. Later psychologists have studied related ideas, such as credibility, warmth, and competence, with more precise methods. For your own life, the passage suggests a practical question. What gives the people you trust their influence over you? If it is consistency, honesty, and a record of being right, that is a good sign. If it is only confidence and charm, it is worth looking a little closer before you follow their lead.

sections.title: All or nothing
sections.narration: Le Bon also describes how groups handle ideas. He writes that crowds are only cognisant of simple and extreme sentiments, and that the opinions, ideas, and beliefs suggested to them are accepted or rejected as a whole, and considered as absolute truths or as not less absolute errors. Picture a debate in which every position becomes all good or all bad. There is no room for a middle view. This is a recognizable habit of heated discussion, especially online. Be careful, though, not to assume that every group behaves this way. Many groups discuss details carefully, and Le Bon himself stresses a particular kind of excited crowd. His observation is better used as a test of your own thinking. When you hold an opinion, can you state what is right about the other side? Can you say which parts of your own position are uncertain? If every part of your view feels equally certain, that is a sign to slow down. Real questions usually come in degrees, and honest answers usually include some doubt.

sections.title: Doubt, strength, and intolerance
sections.narration: Here is one of the sharper observations in the book. Le Bon says that being in doubt as to what constitutes truth or error, and having a clear notion of its strength, a crowd is as disposed to give authoritative effect to its inspirations as it is intolerant. He is saying that uncertainty about the truth, combined with confidence in numbers, can produce intolerance. We might see something like this when a group is unsure of its facts but sure of its power to punish disagreement. Consider how this applies on a small scale. When you are unsure about something but surrounded by people who agree, do you become more forceful, or more careful? Le Bon would predict the first. Modern research gives a more mixed picture, and it finds that groups can also correct their members. So hold the claim lightly, and use it as a personal warning. Doubt should make us more curious. If it makes us louder, something has gone wrong, and it is worth asking what we are protecting.

sections.title: Belonging and borrowed opinions
sections.narration: Le Bon notes that belonging comes with a price. He writes that to belong to a school is necessarily to espouse its prejudices and preconceived opinions. A school here means a group of thinkers with shared assumptions, and the point applies to any community. Joining a team, a profession, or a movement gives us friends and meaning. It also gives us a set of opinions we may never have examined. This is not a reason to avoid belonging. Almost everyone needs it. It is a reason to know what you have borrowed. Try an exercise. Choose one opinion you share with your closest group, and trace how you came to hold it. Did you read the arguments, or did you absorb it from the people around you? Neither answer is shameful. The difference is that an opinion you have examined is yours, and you can defend or revise it. An opinion you have only inherited belongs to the group, and it tends to break when someone challenges it.

sections.title: Prestige repeated becomes power
sections.narration: We have followed Le Bon through six ideas: prestige as domination, its two kinds, prestige without fortune, all-or-nothing opinion, doubt and intolerance, and the price of belonging. One sentence connects them. He writes that great power is given to ideas propagated by affirmation, repetition, and contagion by the circumstance that they acquire in time that mysterious force known as prestige. In plain terms, an idea that is repeated by respected voices begins to feel true on its own. Remember the limits of this book. It is an 1895 theory by an author who feared mass movements, and later scholars have criticized its sweeping claims. Read the original chapters and judge for yourself. The useful ending is a precise question. Which idea do you trust mainly because it has been repeated by people you respect, and what evidence would you need to keep trusting it? Write down one answer, and subscribe to MindLore for psychology read from the original texts.
